identity.title: Central line exit-site erythema, tenderness, or purulence (with line-day count)

technique.how: Remove the dressing and inspect the insertion/exit site for erythema (extent), tenderness on palpation, induration, swelling and purulent drainage; record catheter type (short-term noncuffed vs tunneled/dialysis), site and line-days. For tunneled catheters, palpate along the tunnel for tenderness or expressible pus.
technique.prerequisites: Clean technique for dressing removal; know insertion date and catheter type.
technique.contraindications: None; never delay paired blood cultures for the inspection.

interpretation.positive_finding: Purulence or overt inflammation should raise suspicion of catheter-related BSI, particularly S. aureus or Gram-negative infection in a febrile or septic patient. Even infected short-term CVCs usually look normal, so a positive site is uncommon but meaningful.
interpretation.negative_finding: A normal-appearing site does not exclude catheter-related bloodstream infection; in short-term noncuffed CVCs the sensitivity of local inflammation was 0–3% (PMID 12483050, Abstract). Rely on paired blood cultures.
interpretation.pitfalls: Most CRBSIs are coagulase-negative staphylococci, which incite little local inflammation. Adhesive/dressing dermatitis mimics infection, and tunneled/dialysis catheter exit-site data differ from the short-term CVC study.
interpretation.changes_what: Purulence → culture drainage, paired blood cultures, remove line, treat; normal site → still draw paired cultures if febrile without another source.

sources.citation: Safdar N, Maki DG. Inflammation at the insertion site is not predictive of catheter-related bloodstream infection with short-term, noncuffed central venous catheters. Critical care medicine 2003. Crit Care Med 2002;30(12):2632-5 (PubMed year field 2003).

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use a clean-looking site to rule out line sepsis in a febrile or hypotensive patient with a central line.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Purulence at the site with fever or hypotension: treat as CRBSI — paired cultures, remove the catheter, empiric antibiotics.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Site inflammation was scored by research nurses on a 0–5 scale; no interobserver statistics reported in the abstract.

extraction_notes: Anchor PMID 12483050 confirmed (title matches). No PMC full text; abstract only. The abstract reports sensitivity of local inflammation for CVC-related BSI only as a RANGE across inflammatory variables — quote: "The sensitivity of local inflammation for diagnosis of CVC-related BSI was dismal (0-3%)" (Abstract, Results) — so no point sensitivity can be entered (no-ranges rule); specificity and LRs are not in the abstract. Cohort context (not enterable as an estimate because prevalence alone is not an accuracy field): "Among 1,263 CVCs prospectively studied, 333 (26.3%) were colonized at removal; of these, 35 catheters (2.7%) caused BSIs" (Abstract, Results). Searches ('catheter insertion site inflammation catheter-related bloodstream infection sensitivity'; 'central venous catheter local signs infection sensitivity specificity'; 'hemodialysis catheter exit site infection clinical signs bacteremia predictive value') found no diagnostic-accuracy study of exit-site signs for tunneled/dialysis catheters. Status not_quantified; the anchor is a primary prospective study whose stated conclusion (site appearance cannot be relied on to identify CRBSI) supports the negative_finding wording.
